other_side: Nothing newer had been published, so the counter-source is Monday's essay again — but the half of it that bites on a nine-techniques menu is a different half. Most of the tools on this list sit on one company that, by Zitron's arithmetic, carries over $800bn of compute commitments through 2030, needs $100–200bn a year in fresh capital, and lost $20.9bn on $13.07bn of revenue in 2025; his conclusion is that "at some point, OpenAI will simply not be able to pay its bills". What he sketches for users rather than investors is customers handed "API keys that flow to Microsoft AI Foundry", the free ChatGPT tier stripped back, and no further training of the models people had built their week around. He is not arguing that voice mode or computer history fail to work — he is arguing the entity underwriting them may not be there to keep them working.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is durability: whether tools you build habits on this autumn still exist, at the same price and capability, in two years. Both accept the features work now and that the firms shipping them lose money at scale. The empirical question that resolves is whether OpenAI closes its next raise, and the observable that settles it is the terms — a round at or above the $852bn mark by roughly March 2027, versus a down round, a Microsoft absorption, or a quiet rescue. The residue is worldview: Whittemore treats capability as the thing that compounds and financing as someone else's problem; Zitron treats financing as what determines whether capability survives. Whittemore is vindicated if the money arrives and these techniques become ordinary; Zitron if a funding failure strands them. Both are polemicists with incentives — Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — and the signal is where they agree despite opposite priors: none of this is yet paid for by the people using it. Watch the next raise, and its price.
